The first time I understood that time has weight, I was standing in a hallway that didn’t belong to any particular place. It was just long enough to feel like a boundary between “before” and “after,” and just dim enough that the corners seemed to hold their breath. I remember waiting for something—someone, maybe—and realizing that waiting is not empty. It’s filled with small calculations: how many steps to the bench, whether the light above flickers like it’s trying to confess, what thoughts you can afford before they turn heavy.

When the door finally opened, it wasn’t dramatic. No gust of wind, no sudden music. Just an ordinary swing, as if the world had been quietly going about its business the whole time. And yet my body responded like it had been braced for weather. My shoulders rose. My attention sharpened. The moment arrived wearing a plain face, and that made it more powerful. I felt, briefly, how easily we miss the important events because they don’t announce themselves.

Later, I tried to trace that feeling back to something reasonable. I told myself it was anticipation, or relief, or the brain’s talent for stitching meaning onto sensation. But the truth was simpler: I had been reminded that moments pass, but they also leave deposits. They linger in how we stand, in what we expect, in the soft ways our hope learns new shapes.

If time has weight, then memory is the scale.
